items.title: Choose a representation that exposes the relationship
items.chapter_title: Read the question into a useful model
items.transcript: This section is called Choose a representation that exposes the relationship. A line is useful for order, ranks and intervals. When counting objects between two endpoints, distinguish the objects from the gaps separating them. Inclusive counting keeps both endpoints; strict counting keeps neither. For a queue described from opposite ends, first translate both descriptions into positions measured from one end. A007 is a place to practise keeping those counting conventions consistent. SEE IT Marks and the gaps between them Keeping the endpoints gives six marks. Removing both endpoints gives four marks. Measuring along the same line counts five gaps. A table is useful when several categories must be compared. Put the same kind of quantity in each column, and give the headings units. A drawing is useful when adjacency, parallel sides or a boundary matters. It should record stated facts rather than guessed measurements. An equation is useful when equal totals or repeated changes can be described compactly. Often two representations work together: the picture explains why an equation is true. Choose the smallest representation that keeps every restriction. A large drawing can hide a simple relationship; an over-short equation can hide an assumption. If you remove information, explain why it cannot affect the answer. A folded object, for instance, may require a model of which pieces remain connected. A065 rewards reading that physical structure instead of applying a rule remembered from an ordinary open book. Before moving on, open your notebook. items.transcript: Here is a worked teaching example for Read the question into a useful model. Read a ruler as distances A ribbon starts at the 2 cm mark of a ruler and ends at the 9 cm mark. How long is the ribbon? Explain what is being counted. The ribbon’s endpoints line up with 2 and 9. The seven intervals between them supply the length. Work through the example 1. items.title: Find an invariant by inspecting one move
items.chapter_title: Follow what changes and what stays fixed
items.transcript: This section is called Find an invariant by inspecting one move. An invariant is a quantity that does not change when a permitted move is made. It might be a total, a difference, a product, a remainder or a colour balance. Start by comparing the state immediately before and immediately after one move. A claim about a long process becomes much easier to justify if every individual move preserves the same quantity. SEE IT Two moves, two different invariants A transfer moves existing units between piles, so their total stays fixed. Adding two new units to each pile preserves the difference instead. A transfer between two piles preserves their combined total. If t is transferred from the first pile to the second, the signed difference “first minus second” decreases by 2t. To find the absolute gap, also check whether the piles exchange order. By contrast, adding the same amount to both piles preserves their difference but changes their total. Naming the operation prevents these two situations from being confused. A038 and A112 are useful places to look for a preserved difference rather than solve several unrelated unknowns. If objects come in two types with different per-object contributions, compare the real collection with a starting model made entirely from one type. Keep the object count fixed. Each replacement changes the total by the same difference, so the total change determines how many replacements occurred. Check both the object count and the final total. A014 and A056 fit this comparison method. Sometimes the visible entries are not the quantities worth tracking. Try a small adjustment such as adding or subtracting a fixed amount from each entry. Expand the rule and look for cancellation or factorisation. N1.26 invites this kind of search. The important proof has two parts: identify a candidate quantity, then show algebraically that one legal move leaves it unchanged. A pattern noticed in a few trials is only a clue. items.title: Reverse operations in the opposite order
items.chapter_title: Follow what changes and what stays fixed
items.transcript: This section is called Reverse operations in the opposite order. Suppose a rule multiplies an input by a nonzero number a and then adds b. Its output is y=ax+b. To recover x, undo the final addition first, obtaining y-b, then divide by a. The reverse rule is x=(y-b)/a. Reversing the individual operations while keeping their original order generally fails because each operation acts on a different current quantity. SEE IT Read the reverse arrows from the output The final forward operation is +3. Undo that first with -3, then undo  times 4 with  divided by 4. A fraction of what remains must be applied to the current whole. If a process keeps fractions r and s in successive stages, the final amount is rs times the start. Provided neither kept fraction is zero, divide by the combined multiplier to recover the start. A011 is useful for following the changing whole. Write the amount after each stage if the words make it easy to lose track. Reversal also reveals restrictions. If the story involves whole objects, every reconstructed intermediate amount must be a whole number and each required move must be possible. A backward calculation that reaches the final target but requires an impossible earlier state is invalid. A015 combines reverse thinking with such restrictions; checking the forward journey is part of the solution, not merely an optional second calculation. Before moving on, open your notebook. items.title: Compare different orders of the same operations
items.chapter_title: Follow what changes and what stays fixed
items.transcript: This section is called Compare different orders of the same operations. Operations do not always commute: changing their order can change the result. To compare two orders, apply both to a general starting value x. Simplify the two expressions and subtract them. The sign of the difference tells you which order is better, while cancellation may show that the comparison does not depend on the starting value at all. For a longer chain, compare neighbouring operations first. If swapping a pair improves the result, ask whether later operations preserve that improvement. Multiplication by a positive number does; multiplication by a negative number reverses it. This detail matters when turning a local comparison into a claim about a whole sequence. A142 develops the idea of proving a good order through justified exchanges. Keep invariants and optimization separate. An invariant may show that every legal route ends at the same value. An exchange argument may instead show that one route is best. Neither follows merely from testing several orders. Before concluding, state what your calculation proves: sameness across all moves, recoverability of a starting state, or an improvement under a particular swap. items.transcript: Here is a worked teaching example for Follow what changes and what stays fixed. Compare the two orders Start with any non-negative whole number x. Rule A adds 3 and then multiplies by 4. Rule B multiplies by 4 and then adds 3. Which output is larger, and by how much? The bars represent copies of an amount, not a scale drawing of an unknown x. The three additional gold blocks explain the constant difference. Work through the example 1. Rule A makes four copies of x+3, so its output is 4(x+3)=4x+12. 2. Rule B makes four copies of x and adds just one 3, so its output is 4x+3. 3. Both outputs contain the same four copies of x. Rule A has three extra copies of 3: (4x+12)-(4x+3)=9. 4. For a check, x=0 gives outputs 12 and 3. The algebra explains why the same difference holds for every permitted starting value. Answer. Rule A always gives an output 9 larger than Rule B. items.title: Read a remainder as a precise statement
items.chapter_title: Remainders turn long lists into short systems
items.transcript: This section is called Read a remainder as a precise statement. For a positive divisor d, every whole number N can be written N=qd+r, where q is a whole number and 0≤r<d. The remainder r records what is left after q complete groups of size d. Two numbers have the same remainder exactly when their difference is a multiple of d. This difference test is often more useful than calculating either quotient. SEE IT A remainder is the unfinished group Three complete groups of five account for fifteen counters. Two remain, and two is smaller than the group size five. For a repeating list, first decide whether position counting begins at zero or one. A zero remainder means a complete number of cycles has been used; in a list labelled from one, that often points to the last item of the cycle. A repeating process may also have a beginning that never repeats. Mark the first true repeat before reducing a distant position to a remainder. Several remainder conditions must hold at once. Turn them into a short candidate list or compare their differences. If conditions say that a number is the same fixed amount short of several multiples, adding that amount creates a common multiple. A004 and A086 reward keeping all conditions active. Finding a number that satisfies only one divisibility clue does not make it a solution. Before moving on, open your notebook. items.title: Separate the first coincidence from the repeat period
items.chapter_title: Remainders turn long lists into short systems
items.transcript: This section is called Separate the first coincidence from the repeat period. When two processes repeat, a common multiple of their periods describes a possible gap between coincidences. It does not automatically give the first coincidence if their starting positions differ. Track the offset as well as the period. In a clock problem, also identify what counts as the same display: the physical hands or digits may repeat before the full date does. SEE IT The first match is not always the period A starts at time 1 and repeats every 4 units. B starts at time 3 and repeats every 6. They first meet at 9; later meetings are 12 units apart. The least common multiple is the smallest positive number divisible by all the required periods. It is useful because any later repeated joint state must respect every separate cycle. Prime factors, developed in the next chapter, give a systematic way to find it. A022 and A069 require the periods themselves to be interpreted correctly before they are combined. A full calculation is sometimes unnecessary. Parity means the remainder after division by two. If one process can occupy only even positions and another only odd positions, they cannot coincide. Similar contradictions work with other divisors. Look for a remainder that the rules force but the target forbids. This is an impossibility proof: it rules out every attempted construction at once. items.title: Build guarantees with the pigeonhole principle
items.chapter_title: Remainders turn long lists into short systems
items.transcript: This section is called Build guarantees with the pigeonhole principle. The pigeonhole principle says that if more objects than boxes are placed into boxes, some box contains at least two objects. The challenge is usually choosing useful boxes. Remainder classes provide one choice. Two values in the same remainder class have a difference divisible by the divisor, converting a collision of categories into a mathematical relationship. Running totals are especially useful for consecutive blocks. Include the empty running total before any entries are added. Subtracting an earlier total from a later total leaves exactly the entries between them. In N4.26, the categories belong to the running totals, not directly to the individual entries. This change of viewpoint is what connects repeated remainders to a consecutive block. Other boxes can be built from a shared structural feature. N3.27 uses a factor-based classification rather than ordinary remainder boxes. After proving that a certain number of choices is sufficient, check whether it is the smallest guaranteed number. You need a construction showing that one fewer can fail. A guarantee and a sharp guarantee are different achievements, and the second needs both halves of the argument. items.transcript: Here is a worked teaching example for Remainders turn long lists into short systems. Make a guaranteed pair Explain why any four different whole numbers must include two whose positive difference is a multiple of 3. The numbers are sorted by remainder, not by their sizes. Matching remainders make the remainders cancel when the numbers are subtracted. Work through the example 1. On division by 3, every number has exactly one of three remainders: 0, 1 or 2. Use those as three boxes. 2. Four numbers cannot all occupy different boxes. At least two have the same remainder r. 3. Write those two numbers as 3a+r and 3b+r, with a>b. Their difference is 3(a-b), a positive multiple of 3. 4. For example, 2, 6, 10 and 13 enter the boxes shown. The pair 10 and 13 shares remainder 1, and 13-10=3. The boxes prove the claim for every four-number choice, not only this example. Answer. Such a pair always exists because four numbers must repeat one of the three remainders. items.title: Factor with a purpose
items.chapter_title: Use prime factors as the building blocks
items.transcript: This section is called Factor with a purpose. A prime is a whole number greater than one with exactly two positive divisors: one and itself. The number one is not prime. Every whole number greater than one has a prime a factorisation that is unique apart from the order of its factors. items.chapter_title: Use prime factors as the building blocks
items.transcript: This section is called Count divisors by making independent choices. Suppose N=pa qb, where p and q are different primes. A divisor chooses how many copies of p to use, from zero through a, and independently how many copies of q to use, from zero through b. There are a+1 choices of the first exponent and b+1 of the second. Therefore N has (a+1)(b+1) positive divisors. The same reasoning extends to more prime factors. SEE IT Give every divisor an address A column chooses zero, one or two copies of 2. A row chooses zero or one copy of 3. Each cell multiplies those choices, so each divisor appears exactly once. The zero choices matter: choosing no copies of any prime gives the divisor one. Choosing every available copy gives N itself. Each exponent selection produces exactly one divisor, and every divisor must arise this way. These two facts explain why multiplying the choice counts neither misses nor repeats anything. A077 is a good place to connect an exponent count with an organised list of factor pairs. Pairing a divisor d with N/d gives another useful view. Usually the two partners differ. They coincide only when d is the square root of N. Consequently a number has an odd number of positive divisors precisely when it is a perfect square. The special middle divisor is counted once, not twice. This argument includes the number one and avoids treating it as an unexplained exception. Before moving on, open your notebook. items.transcript: This section is called Track prime copies through several conditions. A positive whole number is a perfect square exactly when every exponent in its prime factorisation is even. This turns a product-square condition into a parity question about exponents. The actual product may be enormous, but only whether each exponent is odd or even may matter. SEE IT Compare prime copies, one prime at a time A common divisor can use only the copies both numbers possess. A common multiple must contain enough copies for each number. For a common divisor, no exponent can exceed what every number contains, so the greatest common divisor takes the smallest available exponent. items.title: Decide whether order belongs to the outcome
items.chapter_title: Count outcomes once, using complete cases
items.transcript: This section is called Decide whether order belongs to the outcome. If positions or roles are different, exchanging two objects usually creates a new outcome. If only membership matters, exchanging the order in which members were chosen does not. Write that distinction explicitly. Selecting people for named jobs is different from selecting an unranked team. In A126, the wording determines which choices have order and which do not. SEE IT Explain why division by two works For the three different objects A, B and C, each two-object group has two orders. The six ordered choices merge in equal-sized groups of two. For n different objects in a row, there are n choices for the first place, n-1 for the second, and so on. Their product is written n!, pronounced “n factorial”. To select an unordered pair, the ordered count n(n-1) counts every pair twice, once in each order, so divide by two. The justification for division is equal repeated counting, not a vague sense that the first total is too large. More generally, C(n, k) denotes the number of ways to choose k different objects from n different objects when order does not matter. For integers 0 ≤ k ≤ n, first count ordered selections: n(n-1)⋯(n-k+1). Each selected group appears in k! orders, so C(n, k) = n!/[k!(n-k)!]. There is one empty selection, so C(n, 0) = 1 and 0! = 1. If k > n, there is no such selection and C(n, k) = 0. Repeated objects need the same care. Temporarily labelling identical objects makes them different, which may overcount the printed arrangements. Before dividing, establish how many labelled versions every unlabelled arrangement has. If that number varies from outcome to outcome, one division cannot repair the count. A099 and N4.28 give useful practice in deciding whether the object being counted is an arrangement, an operation history or a final result. Before moving on, open your notebook. items.transcript: This section is called Split by the restriction that changes the choices. A useful case division has two properties: the cases cannot overlap, and together they cover every legal outcome. Choose a feature that controls the remaining choices. In a digit problem, the last digit or the position of zero may be more restrictive than the first digit. Fixing that feature can turn a confusing count into several straightforward products. SEE IT A complement needs a visible universe Each switch has two states, so the universe has four complete outcomes. Only ON, ON is forbidden; subtracting it leaves three. Multiply within a case when successive choices build one complete outcome. Add across disjoint cases. Do not assume every case has the same number of choices. A leading-zero rule, a required neighbour or a fixed position can make one branch smaller than another. Sometimes it is easier to count everything and subtract the forbidden outcomes. This complement method needs a clear universe: what exactly is included in “everything”? If two forbidden conditions can occur together, subtracting their counts separately may remove an outcome twice. Either separate them into disjoint classes or restore the overlap. A048 is a place to compare direct counting with a carefully defined complement. Before moving on, open your notebook. items.transcript: This section is called Prove that the classification is reversible. A strong counting method gives each outcome an address in your list of cases. From an outcome, you should be able to recover the choices that produced it. Conversely, every allowed choice in the method should build a valid outcome. This two-way check proves completeness and prevents double counting. It is often more convincing than a second long multiplication. Neighbour restrictions can sometimes be handled by placing separator objects first and using the gaps around them. Restrictions on misplaced objects can be handled by describing how positions send objects around cycles. N2.26 and N1.27 develop these different representations. Be especially careful when several action histories can produce one final object. Classify the final structures, or identify precisely which histories merge together. N4.28 asks for this distinction. For an independent check, list the smallest meaningful cases or use a different classification. A computer enumeration can confirm a count, but the written explanation should still make clear why every legal outcome has one place in the argument. Before moving on, open your notebook. items.transcript: Here is a worked teaching example for Count outcomes once, using complete cases. Let the restriction split the cases A lunch contains one sandwich, cheese or bean, and one fruit, apple, pear or plum. Cheese may not be paired with plum. How many different legal lunches are there? items.chapter_title: Count the same structure from two directions
items.transcript: This section is called Count incidences before counting objects. An incidence is a meeting between an object and one of its features: a bridge and an endpoint, a shape and an edge, or a member and a group. You do not need to remember the word to use the idea. Ask what is being counted when each local object reports its own contribution, and how many reports refer to the same underlying thing. SEE IT Every edge reports at two ends The graph has five edges. Its four vertices report degrees 3, 2, 3 and 2, totalling ten because each edge meets two vertices. In a network where every edge joins two vertices, adding all vertex degrees counts each edge twice. The degree of a vertex is the number of edges meeting it. Thus the degree total equals twice the edge count. The same reasoning explains why the degree total is even. An odd total is impossible, regardless of how many different drawings have been tried. For a solid assembled from faces, adding the face-edge counts may count shared edges twice. For a row of joined objects, a new object may share part of the previous boundary. A074 and A096 reward tracking which pieces are genuinely new. The useful count is determined by the joining rule, not by multiplying the size of one separate object by the number of objects. Before moving on, open your notebook. items.transcript: This section is called Give each component its contribution. Suppose several measurements each include some of the same unknown quantities. Adding the measurements can be useful if every unknown appears equally often. Then the sum is a fixed multiple of the desired total. If one unknown appears more often, the extra contribution must be kept rather than silently discarded. A076 and A132 develop these related forms of bookkeeping. items.transcript: This section is called Turn contribution limits into a sharp bound. If every proposed group uses a fixed number of pairs, and no pair may be reused, the available pairs place an upper bound on the number of groups. A bound is only half an optimization solution. It proves that exceeding a number is impossible, but does not prove that the number can be reached. After obtaining the bound, construct an arrangement and check every rule. In a group-design problem, verify that no pair is repeated; in a scheduling problem, verify that no participant has conflicting assignments. A list that looks orderly can still conceal a repeated pair. Local counting can also reveal hidden global information. Different kinds of events may distribute different total contributions, so a known grand total determines how many events of each kind occurred. N2.27 combines this observation with a further restriction on a selected group. A139 similarly rewards noticing unequal incidences before trying placements. The general habit is to count contributions first and use the resulting structure to guide the construction. Before moving on, open your notebook. items.transcript: This section is called Build an honest sample space. A sample space is the collection of possible complete outcomes. items.transcript: This section is called Read decimal places as divisibility conditions. A terminating decimal with at most k places is an integer divided by 10k. Therefore multiplying it by 10k gives an integer. This is a useful test because it turns a statement about written digits into a divisibility condition. Leading zeros after the decimal point still occupy places; trailing zeros can be removed without changing the value. SEE IT Build a power of ten from prime partners Forty supplies three 2s but only one 5. Two additional 5s pair with the unpaired 2s, making three factors of 10. Multiply the numerator by the same 25 to preserve the fraction. In lowest terms, a fraction terminates exactly when its denominator contains no primes except two and five. Every power of ten is built from those primes. If the reduced denominator has only those factors, multiplying by enough missing copies turns it into a power of ten. If another prime remains, no power of ten can supply it. Cancellation must happen before applying this test. For a positive integer k, exactly k decimal places means at most k places but not at most k-1 places after unnecessary trailing zeros are removed. N4.27 develops this distinction. It is often cleaner to count the broader divisibility condition and subtract the smaller one. For decimal shifts, track the place-value multiplier instead of moving a written point without explanation. A119 rewards interpreting the change as an exact fraction of the shifted quantity. items.transcript: This section is called Classify game positions by their legal moves. In a finite take-away game, call a position winning if the player about to move can force a win against every response. Call it losing if that player cannot. These statements describe perfect play, not a prediction about what an inexperienced opponent might choose. It may produce a perpendicular height, an isosceles triangle or two triangles with a shared base. Explain why the line helps before calculating. Adding many unrelated lines can make a diagram harder to read without creating any usable information. Coordinates offer another exact representation. Choose axes that match existing horizontal or vertical structure, then describe points by their positions. Differences of coordinates describe movement between points. Equal coordinate changes can establish parallel directions; fixed horizontal or vertical lines reveal perpendicular distances. The coordinates are a model of the stated geometry, so choosing them must not introduce an unproved midpoint, equality or right angle. For any points X, P and Y, the triangle inequality says XP + PY ≥ XY. Equality holds exactly when P lies on the straight segment from X to Y. Three positive lengths form a nondegenerate triangle exactly when each is shorter than the sum of the other two; for lengths ordered a ≤ b ≤ c, it is enough to check a + b > c. A reflection preserves distances, and every point on its mirror line stays fixed. Reflecting one endpoint can therefore turn a shortest broken route through a line into a straight-segment problem. Lattice diagrams require an additional distinction: a segment may pass through grid points between its endpoints. A059 is a place to examine that structure instead of counting only visible endpoint pairs. items.chapter_title: Turn routes and schedules into networks
items.transcript: This section is called Use future obligations to reject tempting moves. When a route must visit many locations without repetition, a locally legal move may make the final goal impossible. After a proposed move, inspect what remains. Can every unvisited location still be reached? Has a location become cut off? Does a branch have only one usable connection left, forcing it to be an endpoint? These are necessary conditions that can eliminate choices early. SEE IT A local obligation can prove impossibility To visit all four vertices exactly once, each degree-one vertex would have to be an endpoint. There are three such vertices, but a path has only two endpoints, so no route works. A route required to visit every vertex exactly once is often called a Hamiltonian path. The name does not supply a formula. The useful reasoning comes from the particular network: narrow passages, dead ends, forced neighbours and separations. A128 and A144 reward explaining why certain continuations must occur, rather than merely presenting one route that happens to work. For a maximum-value route, compare all required omissions with an explicit successful route. For a largest code, examine possible next symbols in descending order but reject a symbol only with a reason that no valid completion exists. A103 combines a route construction with an upper bound on what can be collected. The construction shows possibility; the argument about unavoidable omissions establishes optimality. items.chapter_title: Turn routes and schedules into networks
items.transcript: This section is called Read a schedule as groups of nonconflicting edges. A schedule can also be represented by a network. Participants are vertices and required meetings are edges. If a participant can take part in at most one meeting during a time slot, the edges placed in that slot must have no shared vertex. This turns a verbal conflict rule into a precise structural condition. Count the total required meetings and the maximum number that can fit in one slot. Dividing gives a lower bound on the number of slots, rounded up if necessary. Individual participants can create another lower bound through their own number of required meetings. Use the strongest available bound, but remember that capacity alone does not guarantee a conflict-free schedule. All the required edges must still be placed legally. The attaining schedule must satisfy the rest pattern as well as use every required pair exactly once and avoid conflicts within each day. Rotation or modular labelling can help organise pairings, but the arrangement must also meet every restriction linking consecutive time slots. Verify these properties separately. A042 adds timing conditions to movement rather than pairwise meetings; there the repeating time structure must be read alongside the distance and speed restrictions. items.chapter_title: Use symmetry without losing or repeating cases
items.transcript: This section is called Do not divide by a symmetry count blindly. A symmetry may leave some objects unchanged. Such an object has fewer visibly different orientations than an object with no symmetry. Therefore dividing a raw count by the number of rotations can fail: not every outcome has been counted that many times. Establish equal repetition before using division, just as in ordinary unordered counting. SEE IT Count the distinct appearances of each object Turn each marked square through 0 degrees, 90 degrees, 180 degrees and 270 degrees. The three kinds of marking give 1, 2 and 4 different appearances. Equal numbers of turns do not guarantee equal repetition. For a cube, there are six choices for the upward face and four choices for a neighbouring face to point forward, giving twenty-four rotations. But this does not mean every cube colouring has twenty-four different appearances. Some colourings look unchanged under several rotations. A026 is a place to classify colour patterns carefully instead of dividing the initial selection count by the rotation total. A useful first classification uses properties that rotations cannot change: the number of marked corners on a face, the pattern of adjacencies, or the number of components. Different values of such a property prove two objects different. Equal values do not necessarily prove them the same. items.chapter_title: Keep ratios, rates and averages precise
items.transcript: This section is called Recover totals and interpret averages. For a nonempty finite list of numbers, the arithmetic mean is the sum divided by the number of entries. Find the median after sorting the entries from smallest to largest: with an odd number of entries it is the middle entry; with an even number it is the mean of the two middle entries. Repeated values still occupy separate positions. The range is the largest entry minus the smallest. These statistics describe different features, so equal means and equal ranges do not force equal medians. When a mean is given, recover the sum before combining it with other conditions. Average speed is total distance divided by total time. It is a time-weighted average of the separate speeds, because a speed maintained for longer contributes for more of the journey. Equal distances do not imply equal times. A slower leg can take much longer than a faster leg, so an ordinary mean of the speed labels may give the wrong result. The same principle applies to combined scores and prices. Recover each group's total before combining groups of unequal sizes. For a mixture price, total cost divided by total mass gives the price per unit mass. For an exchange, track the units through each conversion and reverse the rate when travelling in the opposite direction. A020 uses rates supplied within its problem; their role is to connect the currency amounts exactly. Distinguish distance travelled from net displacement. Travelling away and returning uses time and distance even when some of the displacement cancels. A118 rewards accounting for the entire route. After any rate calculation, reconstruct the quantities over the claimed time and check that they satisfy the original total or meeting condition. The check should test the story's relationship, not merely repeat the division that produced the answer. Before moving on, open your notebook. items.chapter_title: Write proofs that leave no hidden cases
items.transcript: This section is called Use counterexamples and contradictions carefully. To disprove a statement claiming that every object has a property, one legal counterexample is enough. The word legal matters: the example must satisfy all the statement's assumptions. An apparent exception outside the allowed set does not refute the claim. When a method fails, ask which assumption it needed; this can turn an error into a more accurate theorem. A contradiction proof begins by assuming the opposite of what you want to establish, then derives an impossibility using the problem's conditions. An odd degree total in an ordinary finite network contradicts the fact that every edge has two endpoints. A proposed equality case may contradict a parity requirement. The final sentence should identify the incompatible facts explicitly, not merely announce that the attempt “does not work”. For truth-and-lie constraints such as A002, assign each speaker a proposed status, then evaluate the exact claim being made. A truth teller's claim must be true and a liar's false. Propagate these requirements, then check every speaker for consistency before accepting an assignment. A failed construction is not a contradiction. It rules out only that construction unless you prove it represents every possibility.
